summary: The IAB's comments on architecture and policy for Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES), which are application-level services like a web proxy transforming content between server and client. It discusses concerns such as consent and visibility. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: OPES describes services that can change or filter content between a website and a user. This IAB memo lists the consent, integrity, notification, addressing, and privacy issues an OPES design should handle. It does not define a protocol or decide whether the work should be chartered.

subtitle: The IAB's considerations for services that transform content inside a network.

tldr.problem: Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) would let application-level intermediaries transform or filter content. That raises questions about consent, integrity, privacy, and how users can detect improper behavior.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB lists architectural and policy considerations that an OPES framework should address, including one-party consent, explicit IP-layer addressing, notification, access to non-OPES content, reference validity, and privacy.
tldr.outcome: This Informational memo recommends issues that OPES documents should address. It does not specify an OPES protocol or recommend whether OPES should be chartered.

today: RFC 3238 is an Informational IAB memo. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the memo defines no protocol.

sections.title: What OPES Services Would Do
sections.content:
Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) are application-level services placed at intermediaries such as web proxy caches. They can transform or filter content, for example by translating a page, adapting content for a limited-bandwidth path, or scanning for viruses.

The IAB wrote this memo about architectural and policy issues raised during discussion of OPES in the IETF. It does not recommend specific solutions, define protocol requirements, or advise whether OPES should be chartered. It identifies concerns that any standardized OPES solution should address.
sections.plainLanguage: An OPES intermediary can change content before it reaches a user. The memo lists issues designers should address when such a service is placed in the network.

sections.title: Consent Does Not Guarantee Integrity
sections.content:
The IAB says an OPES framework standardized in the IETF must require explicit authorization from at least one application-layer endpoint: either the content provider or the client. But one-party consent alone does not protect integrity, because the other endpoint may not know that a service is acting on the content.

The memo expects that an intermediary may be compromised or behave improperly. It recommends designing for end hosts to detect and respond to such behavior. Digital signatures can help users detect changes, but the IAB says additional protection may be desirable.
sections.plainLanguage: At least one endpoint must authorize an OPES service, but that permission alone does not ensure the service behaves correctly. Users and content providers need ways to detect improper changes.

sections.title: Notification, Addressing, and Privacy
sections.content:
The IAB's considerations call for explicit IP-layer addressing of an intermediary and notification that helps content providers and users detect its actions. If a non-OPES version exists at the content provider, the framework must not prevent a user from retrieving it.

OPES documentation should explain how services relate to URI resolution and how they affect references between or within documents. The overall framework must provide a way for users to learn an intermediary's privacy policies, since every intermediary adds another place where transaction privacy could be compromised.
sections.plainLanguage: Users should know when an intermediary acts and should still be able to reach the original content when it exists. They should also be able to learn the intermediary's privacy policy.

sections.title: The IAB's Checklist
sections.content:
The memo gathers its considerations into a checklist for OPES architecture: one-party consent, IP-layer addressing, notification for providers and users, non-blocking access to the original, clear treatment of URI resolution and references, and privacy-policy discovery.

The list is the memo's main output. It guides later design discussion but does not prescribe a particular mechanism for meeting each consideration.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo ends with a checklist of issues an OPES framework must address. It leaves the specific technical solutions open.

items.label: One-party consent
items.desc: Require authorization from the content provider or client.

items.label: IP-layer addressing
items.desc: The end user explicitly addresses the intermediary at the IP layer.

items.label: Provider notification
items.desc: Help providers detect and respond to inappropriate intermediary actions.

items.label: Non-blocking access
items.desc: Do not prevent retrieval of an available non-OPES version.

items.label: URI resolution
items.desc: Describe services as applying after URI resolution.

items.label: Reference validity
items.desc: Define effects on references within and between documents.

items.label: No ad hoc addressing
items.desc: Review needed addressing changes as architecture extensions.

items.label: Privacy
items.desc: Let users determine intermediaries' privacy policies.
